name_jp: 成田国際空港 第1ターミナル
address_jp: 千葉県成田市三里塚字御料牧場1-1
notes: Both ends of the trip: LY91 lands here 13:20 on Thu 22 Oct, LY92 leaves 15:45 on Wed 11 Nov. The Keisei Skyliner platform is Narita Airport Station, directly beneath the terminal, and Skyliners are all-reserved — a ticket is bought at the station counter or machines before boarding. Skyliners run from the airport until 23:00, and the N'EX to Tokyo Station is an independent second mode. The information line is answered 24 hours. The postal address here is the one carried over with the record and is not confirmed by any operator channel — Narita International Airport Corporation publishes no street address for Terminal 1, so it is shown here unverified. The map pin and the phone number both come from the operator.

The Ueno Park end of the museum day — JR Yamanote, Keihin-Tohoku, Joban and the Tohoku, Hokuriku and Joetsu Shinkansen, plus Tokyo Metro Ginza and Hibiya lines below. Two stops from Akihabara on the Yamanote. The Park Exit (公園口) is the one that opens straight onto the museum hill; the Tokyo National Museum is about 10 minutes on foot from it.

address_jp: 〒110-8712 東京都台東区上野公園13-9
notes: Over 120,000 items, 89 National Treasures and 648 Important Cultural Properties, which the museum's own pages call the most significant collection in Japan in both quantity and quality — the Honkan Japanese galleries, the Heiseikan archaeology halls and the Horyu-ji Treasures building, across a park-sized campus. 9:30–17:00, and to 20:00 on Fridays and Saturdays with last admission 19:30; the visit is Sat 24 Oct, so the evening is available. Closed Mondays, except when a Monday is a public holiday, in which case it closes the following weekday. ¥1,000 admits to the standing collection — but the Daitoku-ji 700th-anniversary exhibition ticket already bought (¥2,100, undated) also admits to the standing collection on the day it is used, so nothing further is paid at the gate. The main-gate ticket window can run over 30 minutes at busy times. The phone is the Hello Dial information line.

address_jp: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1
notes: The Tokaido Shinkansen departure for the move to Kyoto on Wed 28 Oct, reached in one stop from Akihabara on the Yamanote. Arriving that way puts him already inside the ordinary JR gates, walking the in-gate central passage toward the Shinkansen transfer gate — the ekiben counters of GRANSTA Tokyo sit directly on that walk, before the transfer gate, so the stop costs no detour and no re-entry.

address_jp: 〒630-8215 奈良県奈良市東向中町29
notes: Kintetsu Nara Line, underground, at the east end of the Higashimuki arcade with the Gyoki fountain plaza above it. It is the closest station to the park — about fifteen minutes on foot east along Noborioji to the Nara National Museum — but it is a different building from JR Nara, about 1.1 km west, and the two are never interchangeable in a leg: the Kyoto legs on 31 October are JR. No operator page could be cited; Kintetsu publishes no per-station page, so the pin and the address are from OpenStreetMap and its Japanese reverse geocode.

The Great Buddha Hall, a National Treasure of the Edo period and one of the largest wooden buildings in the world — 57.0 m across, 50.5 m deep and 48.7 m high, rebuilt in 1709 by the monk Kokei at about six-tenths of the Tenpyo and Kamakura width after the hall burned twice, though its height and depth are the original ones. Inside sits the 14.98 m Rushana Buddha, cast in 749 and a National Treasure of the Nara period, with the Nara-period octagonal bronze lantern standing in front of the hall. Hours are 7:30–17:30 from April to October and 8:00–17:00 from November to March; the times shown are the October ones, and the visit falls on 31 October. Open every day barring an emergency. ¥800 for adults and cash only — and the Hokke-do, the Kaidan-do and the Todai-ji Museum each charge their own ¥800, with no combined ticket on the temple’s own price list. The museum keeps 9:30–17:30 with last entry 17:00 in October, 9:30–17:00 with last entry 16:30 from November. Groups take no booking and none is needed. About 45 minutes to an hour for the hall and the Nandaimon guardians on the way in.

address_jp: 〒630-8212 奈良県奈良市春日野町160
price: Free; ¥700 for the corridor special worship
notes: Founded in 768 by decree of Empress Shotoku as the tutelary shrine of the Fujiwara, and a World Heritage site: four National Treasure sanctuaries, twenty-seven more buildings that are Important Cultural Properties, and some three thousand lanterns, stone along the approach and bronze along the corridors, of which more than half of all the Muromachi-period lanterns surviving in Japan are here. The rebuilding of the sanctuaries every twenty years has now been done sixty times. The worship hall of the main shrine opens 6:30–17:30 from March to October and 7:00–17:00 from November to February — the times shown are the October ones, and the visit falls on 31 October; the shrine’s own site header quotes a looser general figure of 6:00–18:00. Worship at the outer hall is free. The special worship that takes you inside the corridor — past the hanging lanterns to the Chumon gate, the Mikasa-yama worship point and the Fujinami-no-ya lantern room — is 9:00–16:00 and ¥700, and it is closed on the 1st, 11th and 21st of every month and on certain festival days; 31 October is not one of them. The Kokuhoden treasure hall is 10:00–17:00, last entry 16:30, ¥700. The Manyo Botanical Garden, some three hundred plants named in the Manyoshu, is 9:00–16:30 with last entry 16:00 and ¥700, closed Tuesdays from June to March. Amulets, charms and seals are issued from 9:00 until closing. About an hour for the corridors and lantern galleries, half as much again if the special worship is taken.

address_jp: 京都府京都市左京区田中上柳町32-1
notes: Where the Keihan Oto line ends and the Eizan Railway begins — the day arrives here from Tofukuji on the Keihan and leaves for Kurama on the Eizan, about 30 minutes up the mountain with a train every 15 minutes through the afternoon and a last departure from Kurama at 23:04. The Eizan terminus opened in 1925 and its ticket window is open from the first train to the last. The address carried on this record before was Tanaka Shimoyanagi-cho; the operator's own station page gives Tanaka Kamiyanagi-cho 32-1, and the pin has been moved about 200 m onto the station itself, which was previously sitting on Shimogamo-nishi-dori.

address_jp: 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬本町191
notes: The Eizan Railway's Kurama-line terminus and the start of the day on foot: Kurama-dera gives three minutes from here to the Nio-mon gate. Opened 1929, elevation 238.0 m; staff are on duty in the daytime only, with the ticket window open 9:30-16:20. The pin was about 450 m out and sitting up on the temple approach; it has been moved onto the station building.

address_jp: 〒601-1111 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬本町1073
notes: The tutelary shrine of Kurama, standing on the switchback approach a few minutes above Kurama-dera's Nio-mon gate. Its worship hall was rebuilt in 1607 by Toyotomi Hideyori in the wari-haiden form — two halves with a passage running through the middle — and is an Important Cultural Property, a representative Momoyama-period building; the shrine also holds an Important Cultural Property pair of guardian lion-dogs, which its own site calls the only ones in Japan shown holding a child. Several independent accounts state that the designated pair is on deposit at the Kyoto National Museum and that the pair standing beside the hall is a faithful copy made in 1966; the shrine's own site does not mention this, and Kyoto City's register confirms only the designation, so it is reported rather than official. Its great cedar, about 800 years old and 53 m tall, is a Kyoto City Natural Monument. The shrine came here in 940 by imperial order, and the Kurama Fire Festival — one of Japan's three great fire festivals — is its annual rite, held on the night of 22 October, ten days before this visit. Admission is free. The shrine publishes no opening hours of its own on any of its pages, and Kyoto City's official tourism register leaves the hours and closed-day fields blank for it while tagging it free; the window shown here is therefore Kurama-dera's own 9:00-16:15, which is the gate the shrine is reached through and the honest envelope for a visit. About 10-15 minutes: one hall passed through on the way up, seen from outside.

address_jp: 〒601-1111 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬本町1074
notes: The mountain temple above Kurama village, entered at the Nio-mon where the ¥500 mountain fee is collected; the hours shown are the opening of the main hall, the Hondo Kondo, with its Kongosho stone mandala in the court outside. The Reihoden, the temple's own museum two minutes above the main hall, keeps different hours and is the reason the day is front-loaded: 9:00-16:00, ¥200, closed on Tuesdays (the following day when a Tuesday is a holiday) and from 12 December to the end of February. Its third floor holds the National Treasure Bishamonten triad; the first floor is a natural-history room and the second holds temple treasures and the Yosano memorial room. The cable railway — which the temple states is the only railway in Japan licensed under the Railway Business Act that a religious body operates — starts up at 8:40 and makes its last descent at 16:25, for a ¥200 donation, but it lands above Yuki Shrine and the approach is walked instead. The temple calls the path over the ridge to the Nishi-mon gate at Kibune its own Shugyo-no-michi, the training road. Cash only. The pin was about 240 m up the approach from the main hall and has been moved onto it.

address_jp: 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬貴船町
notes: The temple's own route over the ridge, which it calls the Shugyo-no-michi — from the main hall past the Ikitsugi-no-mizu spring, the Sekurabe-ishi stone, the Kinone-michi where the cedar roots lace the path surface, the Osugi Gongen shrine, the Fudo-do and the Yoshitsune-do, to the Mao-den at the inner sanctuary and down to the Nishi-mon gate at Kibune. About 3.9 km and roughly 60-90 minutes, with about 370 m of descent on the Kibune side. It is a forest path of roots and stone, and the temple's own guidance is not to push on after rain or in dim light. Verified open along the whole segment on 30 July 2026 — the closure notices that circulate concern the 582 m summit ridge beyond the temple's route, which is a different path. The temple posts path closures on its own front page, so that channel is worth a look again close to the trip: a three-day hazard-tree closure of the lower switchback approach ran 5-7 August 2026 and had no bearing on this segment. The pin sits on the Kinone-michi itself.

address_jp: 〒601-1112 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬貴船町180
notes: The head shrine of some two thousand water-deity shrines, in a cedar ravine above Kibune. A visit is the Sanshamairi, the round of three: the Hongu, with the spring water welling from the stone wall and the water fortunes that surface writing when floated on it; the Yui-no-yashiro, the middle shrine of Iwanagahime; and the Okunomiya, the founding site, built over a dragon hole counted among the three great ones in Japan, with the boat-shaped stone beside the hall. Coming down off the mountain the round is walked in reverse — Okunomiya, Yui-no-yashiro, Hongu — which is a deliberate inversion of the traditional order and saves a backtrack. Open every day, free. The hours shown are the shrine's own published window for the Hongu, which it gives for 1 May to 30 November — it publishes no winter set. The amulet and seal office keeps 9:00-17:00. The shrine posts single-day changes to these hours on its own news page, so that channel is worth a look close to the trip. The pin was on a ryokan on the Kibune lane and has been moved onto the Hongu.

address_jp: 京都府京都市左京区鞍馬貴船町5-1
notes: Eizan Railway, Kurama line — the station the Kurama-Kibune day walks out to and takes the train home from, about 27 minutes back to Demachiyanagi. The operator gives no telephone number because the station is unstaffed outside the daytime hours, and the ticket window is open 10:00-17:00; opened 1929, elevation 203.8 m. Kibune village is about 2 km up the valley road from here — Kifune Shrine's own site gives roughly 30 minutes on foot and Kurama-dera's gives 40, and Kyoto Bus route 33 runs the same stretch in about five minutes. Walking it down is the plan; the bus is there if the legs are gone.

name_jp: 蓮華王院 三十三間堂
address_jp: 京都府京都市東山区三十三間堂廻町657
notes: A hall 120 m long north to south, its name taken from the thirty-three bays between the pillars of the inner sanctuary — a length without parallel in wooden architecture, and a National Treasure. Founded in 1164 at Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa's wish and endowed by Taira no Kiyomori; the present building is the 1266 rebuilding after fire. Inside stand a thousand life-size standing Thousand-Armed Kannon, the seated central Kannon of 3.35 m by the Kamakura sculptor Tankei, and the twenty-eight attendants — all National Treasures. The Nandaimon gate of 1600, built by Toyotomi Hideyori, and the tiled Taiko-bei wall beside it are Important Cultural Properties. Open every day of the year; last reception is 30 minutes before closing, so 16:30 on this visit. From 16 November to 31 March the hours change to 9:00-16:00 with reception to 15:30 — the times shown here are the 1 April to 15 November set, which is the one in force on the day. Seven minutes on foot from Keihan Shichijo. The temple's own site serves an incomplete certificate chain and cannot be cited as a link, so the source here is Kyoto City's official tourism register, which prints the same hours, fee, street address and telephone number. Only the postal code is missing from that register, and it is left off rather than carried across from a channel that cannot be cited.

address_jp: 京都府京都市北区紫野大徳寺町53
price: Free (main precinct); sub-temple openings charged separately
notes: The head temple of the Daitokuji branch of Rinzai Zen, founded in 1315 and rebuilt after the Onin War by the monk Ikkyu. The seven-hall layout survives complete and in line from the imperial messenger gate north through the Sanmon, the Buddha hall and the Dharma hall — all Important Cultural Properties — to the National Treasure abbot's hall, with the National Treasure Chinese gate from Hideyoshi's Jurakudai in front of it and a dry garden that is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Historic Site. Hideyoshi held Nobunaga's funeral here, and the daimyo sub-temples that followed are why the complex is what it is. Sen no Rikyu's statue in the upper storey he added to the Sanmon in 1589 is said to have been part of what brought Hideyoshi to order his death. What is open is the free walled precinct and its lanes: the Sanmon, the Dharma hall and the abbot's hall are all closed to the public, so the buildings above are seen from outside. Neither the temple nor Kyoto City's official register publishes hours or closed days for the precinct, and the imperial messenger gate is listed as permanently on view — the round-the-clock times shown here describe the open lanes, not a ticketed visit. The visit on this day is Soken-in and Korin-in, two of the four sub-temples opened for the 700th anniversary of the founding, and each carries its own hours and fee. Kotoin has been closed since April 2020. The pin was sitting on Sangen-in, a different sub-temple, and has been moved onto the main complex.

address_jp: 京都府京都市北区紫野大徳寺町59
notes: Oda Nobunaga's memorial temple, built in 1583 by Hashiba Hideyoshi — later Toyotomi — on the first anniversary of Nobunaga's death at Honno-ji, and a move in the succession struggle as much as an act of mourning. The main hall holds the wooden seated statue of Nobunaga that Hideyoshi gave, life-size at about 115 cm, carved by the Kei-school sculptor Yasukiyo and an Important Cultural Property. The front gate and the earthen wall survive from the 1583 founding, the wall built as a parent-and-child wall with a second one inside it. Seven grave markers of Nobunaga and his family stand in the grounds — Nobunaga, his daughter Tokuhime, his consort Nohime and others — and three tea rooms; Hideyoshi set his own tea seat in this temple's abbot's hall at the great Daitoku-ji tea gathering. The camellia in the grounds is about 400 years old. This is a special opening, not a standing one: it runs 10 October to 30 November 2026 and the times shown are the reception, which ends at 16:00. Closed 4 and 5 November and 21 and 22 November, and the operator says more closed days can be added for temple business, so it is worth a look at their page shortly before the trip. Reception starts at 11:30 on 1 November only. ¥800, cash only, and no photography inside the hall. About 7 minutes on foot from the Daitokuji-mae bus stop.

address_jp: 京都府京都市北区紫野大徳寺町80
notes: Founded between 1521 and 1528 by Hatakeyama Yoshisou, military governor of Noto, and named after his posthumous name. It fell into disrepair with his house, and in 1581 Maeda Toshiie re-roofed the main hall and made it his family temple too, so it carries both the Hatakeyama and the Maeda of Kaga. The front gate and the main hall, the Chinese gate included, survive from the founding and are Important Cultural Properties; the hall's roof sits lower than later abbot's halls, which is what gives it its settled, unhurried look, and the Chinese gate keeps the Muromachi wave-pattern lattice and flower-headed windows of Zen building. The dry garden of white sand and stone groupings was restored from documents by Nakane Kinsaku during the hall's dismantling and repair. The tea room is the Kankyotei. A special opening, not a standing one: 5-29 September and 3 October to 15 December 2026, with the times shown being the reception, which ends at 16:30 and moves to 16:00 from 1 December. The only published closed day is 23 September, and the operator says more can be added for temple business. ¥800, cash only; photography is allowed in the garden only. The maples around the main hall colour from late November, after this visit.

address_jp: 広島県広島市南区松原町2番37号
notes: The Midori-no-Madoguchi ticket office is open 5:30 to 22:00, and the Shinkansen transfer counter window 5:30 to 23:15. Coin lockers are among the station’s listed facilities. For a bag too large for a locker, Crosta Hiroshima runs a staffed baggage counter inside the station from 9:00 to 20:00 every day of the year at 1,000 yen a bag, and will deliver a bag to a hotel in the city for 1,500 yen or to the Miyajima area for 2,300 to 2,500 yen; its telephone is 090-2867-4941. Tours Hiroshima, four minutes’ walk from the station, takes bags from 8:30 to 18:00 every day at 500 yen and delivers for 1,000 yen.

address_jp: 〒739-0588 広島県廿日市市宮島町1-1
notes: Open every day of the year, in six seasonal bands. The band 15 October to 30 November is 6:30 to 17:30, which is the one this trip falls in; 1 March to 14 October is 6:30 to 18:00 and 1 to 31 December is 6:30 to 17:00. Admission is 300 yen for an adult, 200 for a high-school student and 100 for a child; the Treasure Hall is another 300 yen and a combined ticket is 500. The Treasure Hall opens 8:00 to 17:00 all year; it was completed in April 1934 and is itself a Registered Tangible Cultural Property, holding a selection of the shrine's treasures and art objects. The main sanctuary complex — honden, heiden and haiden, with the haraiden and its attached takabutai and hirabutai — and the Marodo shrine are National Treasures; the Noh stage is an Important Cultural Property, dated 1680 in the national cultural-property record and built out over the sea, which is why its floor rather than a buried resonating jar carries the sound of the feet — the widely repeated claim that it is the only one in Japan built over the sea appears nowhere on the shrine's own pages and is not asserted here. It began as a stage donated by the Mori in the Warring States period and rebuilt in the Edo period by the Asano lords of Hiroshima. The shrine was founded in 593 by Saeki Kuramoto, and Taira no Kiyomori built the over-water shinden-style complex in about 1168. The corridors run 108 ken east and west together, with the floorboards laid with slight gaps to let water pressure through. The great torii is 16 metres high and weighs about 60 tonnes; its six legs are not buried in the seabed but stand on the gate's own weight. Its repair, begun in June 2019, was completed in December 2022. Two works are running on the shrine's own published schedule: structural reinforcement of the east corridor from 10 April 2024 to December 2026, and repair of the five-storey pagoda from 20 January 2025 to 20 November 2027 — the pagoda is wrapped for the whole of that time. The shrine's construction page prints no visitor consequence for either, and adds that no further works are scheduled.

address_jp: 〒739-0592 広島県廿日市市宮島町210
notes: The gates open 8:00 to 17:00. Neither the temple's own pages nor the prefectural tourism page publishes an admission charge for the precinct — the only prices printed are for taking part in things, such as zazen at 1,000 yen. This is a head temple of the Omuro school of Shingon, under Ninna-ji, founded in 806 after Kukai crossed to Miyajima and practised on Mt Misen; it was the betto temple that conducted the rituals of Itsukushima Shrine and the centre of Buddhist practice on the island, and it still has charge of the site on Misen where Kukai performed the Gumonji rite. It holds the eleven-headed Kannon that once stood in the shrine's inner sanctuary. Beneath the main hall is a kaidan-meguri, a passage walked in complete darkness as a rite of purification and rebirth, and the precinct has an Ichigan Daishi, to whom one wish at a time is addressed. The temple's own account records that Ito Hirobumi paid for the building of the mountain path, valuing the view from the summit of Misen. These coordinates are the temple itself, on the slope above the town.

address_jp: 〒739-0588 広島県廿日市市弥山山頂
notes: The summit is 535 metres. The primeval forest on Misen is a National Natural Monument and forms part of the area inscribed as the World Heritage site of Itsukushima Shrine. Three walking courses run up the mountain through its ruins, great rocks and old-growth forest. The prefectural tourism page gives about two hours on foot from the pier to the top; the alternative is the ropeway, roughly 25 minutes to reach its lower station, a 15-minute ride in two stages, and then about 30 minutes more on foot from the upper station. A free shuttle bus to the lower station runs from 9:50 at about 20-minute intervals. The ropeway itself runs 9:00 to 16:00 going up and 9:20 to 16:30 coming down, at 2,000 yen return or 1,100 yen one way; its only 2026 suspension was 22 June to 16 July for inspection, and the operator posts no closure in October or November. The observatory at the summit is open 10:00 to 16:00; it was rebuilt in 2013 to a design by Hiroshi Sambuichi around the idea of sitting to look at the view, and was given three stars by the Michelin Green Guide in 2015. These coordinates are the summit, not a trailhead and not the ropeway's upper station.

address_jp: 〒739-0588 広島県廿日市市宮島町1-1
notes: Open 8:30 to 16:30 all year, with no closing day; 100 yen for an adult and 50 for a school child. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered the warrior-monk Ankokuji Ekei to build this great sutra hall so that a thousand volumes of sutras could be recited once a month. The prefectural tourism board calls it the largest wooden building on the island — the shrine's own pages make no size claim — and it is known as Senjokaku, the thousand-tatami pavilion, because it is as wide as 857 tatami mats. Work stopped when Hideyoshi died suddenly, so no ceiling was ever laid except above the seat of the deity and the hall stands unfinished to this day. Under the Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism its Buddhist image was moved to Daigan-ji and it became Toyokuni Shrine, enshrining Hideyoshi. The five-storey pagoda beside it — an Important Cultural Property, built in 1407, a little over 29 metres tall with a bark-shingled roof — is under repair from 20 January 2025 to 20 November 2027 and is not viewable as itself during this trip.

address_jp: 〒730-0811 広島県広島市中区中島町1-2
notes: The hours recorded here are the WALK-UP window, not the museum’s published opening hours, and the difference is the one that can refuse entry at the door. The museum publishes 7:30 to 19:00 for September to November, but its ticket office and ticket machines close at 17:30 in that season, and entering the permanent exhibition between 7:30 and 8:30 or between 17:30 and 18:30 requires a reservation made online in advance — during those two bands no ticket is sold at the window or the machine, and only visitors holding a web reservation may enter the paid zone. A walk-up visitor can therefore buy a ticket and enter only between 8:30 and 17:30, which is what the hours here say. Admission to the permanent exhibition is 200 yen for adults and university students, 160 each in a group of 30 or more; 100 yen for high-school students, free in a group of 20 or more; and free for middle-school age and younger. The museum closes only on 30 and 31 December and for a period in mid-February, and the only temporary closure posted for an exhibition changeover is 15 to 20 February 2027, which is after this trip. No October or November 2026 closure, works or changeover is posted.

Opening hours run in two seasonal bands — 9:00 to 18:00 from 16 March to 15 September, and 9:00 to 17:00 from 16 September to 15 March, which is the band this trip falls in. Entry closes 30 minutes before the garden does, so the last entry is 16:30. Admission is 350 yen for a general visitor. The garden closes only from 29 to 31 December. It was laid out from Genna 6 (1620) as the villa garden of Asano Nagaakira, the first Asano lord of Hiroshima, and its designer was his senior retainer Ueda Soko, who was also known as a tea master. It was designated a Place of Scenic Beauty in 1940 under the law then in force for the preservation of historic sites, places of scenic beauty and natural monuments. The atomic bomb of 6 August 1945 took many lives in the garden, reduced the Seifukan and its other buildings to ruins in an instant and burnt its great and famous trees, but the Takuei pond, the artificial hills and the Kokokyo bridge kept their old form despite severe damage. Restoration began in 1949, the garden reopened in April 1951, and the work was substantially complete with the building of the Meigetsutei in November 1974, thirty years after the bombing.
