notes: The base station for both Tokyo legs — JR Yamanote, Keihin-Tohoku and Sobu lines, Tokyo Metro Hibiya line, Tsukuba Express. About 150 m (3 min) from the hotel via the Central Gate. The Nippori transfer runs from the JR platforms, 4 stops.

address_jp: 〒110-0007 東京都台東区上野公園7-7
notes: The Le Corbusier main building is itself the UNESCO World Heritage listing, so the architecture is half the visit. About 10 minutes on foot across Ueno Park from the Tokyo National Museum. Open to 20:00 on Fridays and Saturdays — the visit is Sat Oct 24 — and closed Mondays, except when a Monday is a national holiday, in which case it closes the following weekday instead. Last admission is 30 minutes before closing. ¥500 covers the permanent collection; special exhibitions are ticketed separately. The phone is the Hello Dial information line.

address_jp: 〒110-0001 東京都台東区谷中3丁目
notes: A short shitamachi shopping street of about sixty small shops, entered down the Yuyake-dandan steps on the Nippori side. There is no single opening time — every shop keeps its own hours — and the street itself is a public road, walkable at any hour. The merchants’ association office is at Yanaka 3-9-15.

A Tokyo metropolitan cemetery opened in 1874, 102,537 m2, crossed by a cherry-lined central avenue. The paths are public and open at any hour — there is no gate. About 5-6 minutes on foot from Nippori Station. The phone and the 8:30-17:30 window belong to the management office (paperwork to 16:30), not to the grounds.

The 1706 ensemble — honden, heiden, haiden, karamon and romon — survives intact and is an Important Cultural Property. The Otome-Inari vermilion torii tunnel and the pond garden are the walk; the precinct is compact. Karamon gate hours are seasonal on the shrine’s own table: 5:30–17:30 in October, 6:00–17:00 from November. The hours shown here are October’s, because the visit is Sat Oct 24. The amulet office runs 9:30–17:00 in October, 9:30–16:30 from November. Open daily.

address_jp: 〒193-0844 東京都八王子市高尾町
notes: Terminus of the Keio Takao line and the trailhead itself — Trail 1 begins a few minutes from the ticket gate, so there is no bus to catch at either end of the hike. About 50 minutes from Shinjuku. The cable car and chairlift base stations are up the approach, and TAKAO 599 MUSEUM is 4 minutes away.

address_jp: 東京都八王子市高尾町
notes: The 599 m summit inside Meiji-no-mori Takao Quasi-National Park — a viewing deck over the Kanto plain and, on a clear day, Mt Fuji. The plan walks up Trail 1, the paved graded route through cedar forest past Yakuo-in, and descends Trail 6 through the Biwa-taki valley, unpaved and beside a stream: roughly three hours of walking on gentle surfaces. The cable car runs in both directions if the legs give out, but walking is the plan. These coordinates are the summit, not the trailhead.

address_jp: 〒193-8686 東京都八王子市高尾町2177
notes: A working Shingon mountain temple about two-thirds of the way up Trail 1 — the Nio-mon, the main hall, the Gongen-do and the okunoin, with the tengu statues the mountain is known for. The precinct sits on the open mountain and the temple publishes no gate hours, which is why no open/closed badge is shown; the 9:00–16:00 window is its telephone reception. Roughly an hour on foot above the station, then 30 minutes more to the summit.

address_jp: 〒193-0844 東京都八王子市高尾町2435-3
notes: The mountain’s free interpretation centre, beside Takaosanguchi station — Mt Takao’s plants and animals, and the fallback if the hike is rained off or the indoor Tokyo days are shut. Hours are 8:00–17:00 from April to November (last entry 16:30) and 8:00–16:00 from December to March; the hours shown are the April–November set, which covers the Oct 26 visit. Open year-round apart from scheduled maintenance days.

address_jp: 〒247-0062 神奈川県鎌倉市山ノ内
notes: Where the Kamakura day starts — JR Yokosuka line and Shonan-Shinjuku line, about an hour from central Tokyo. Engaku-ji’s entrance is a minute from the platform, Tokei-ji 4 minutes, and Meigetsu-in and Kencho-ji lie further down the same road south.

address_jp: 〒247-0062 神奈川県鎌倉市山ノ内409
notes: Open daily — there is no weekly closing day. 8:30–16:30 from March to November, to 16:00 from December to February; the hours shown are the March–November set, which covers the Oct 27 visit. A hillside compound of about thirty sub-temples: the great Sanmon, the Butsuden, and up its own flight of steps the Ogane, a National Treasure bell of 1301 that can be seen on any day. The Shariden is shown close up only Nov 1–3.

address_jp: 神奈川県鎌倉市山ノ内189
notes: The round-window temple, on the lane between Engaku-ji and Kencho-ji. 9:00–16:00; the hours change only in June, for the hydrangeas. The main grounds and the Satori-no-mado window stand year-round. The rear garden opens separately in June and again for the late-November maples, for another ¥500 — it is not open on Oct 27. The temple keeps no official website of its own; the source here is the Kamakura City Tourist Association.

address_jp: 〒247-8525 神奈川県鎌倉市山ノ内8
notes: Head temple of the Kamakura Five Mountains, founded 1253 — the Sanmon, the Butsuden, the Hojo and the Kara-mon, and beside the Sanmon a second National Treasure bell, cast 1255 and always visible. 8:30–16:30; admission ¥500, cash only. About 15 minutes on foot from Kita-Kamakura station, 5 by bus. The climb to Hanso-bo and the Shojoken viewpoint — around 250 steps, then 180 more — starts from the rear of the precinct. These coordinates are the entrance on the main road; the grounds run a long way uphill behind it.

address_jp: 〒247-0062 神奈川県鎌倉市山ノ内1367
notes: The substitution to lead with if rain shortens the day — 4 minutes from Kita-Kamakura station, on the same street as everything else. 9:00–16:00. No admission is charged; the temple asks instead that visitors pay respects at the main hall and leave an offering. Its treasure house closes on the 1st and 3rd Tuesdays of the month — Oct 27 is the fourth Tuesday, so it is open. Photography is restricted inside the grounds.

address_jp: 〒248-8588 神奈川県鎌倉市雪ノ下2-1-31
notes: Kamakura’s central shrine and the walk-out endpoint of the day, downhill from Kencho-ji and about 10 minutes on foot from Kamakura station’s east exit. The precinct is open 6:00–20:00 year-round — the shrine prints this as a single all-year figure — and there is no admission. The museums inside the grounds keep their own hours: the Treasure Hall 9:00–16:00, the Kamakura Bunkakan 10:00–16:30 and closed Mondays.

address_jp: 〒248-0006 神奈川県鎌倉市小町一丁目
notes: The way home at the end of the Kamakura day — JR Yokosuka and Shonan-Shinjuku lines, about an hour back to central Tokyo, and the Enoden terminus alongside. Tsurugaoka Hachimangu is 10 minutes on foot from the east exit.

address_jp: 〒130-0015 東京都墨田区横網一丁目
notes: The sumo district — JR Sobu line, and the Toei Oedo line station of the same name a few minutes south. The Edo-Tokyo Museum is beside the JR west exit and the chanko restaurants are in the streets around it.

Tokyo’s oldest surviving Edo daimyo garden, begun 1629 by the Mito Tokugawa, and both a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Special Historic Site — the only garden in Tokyo to hold the two together. A wa-kan landscape of Japanese and Chinese scenes: the Engetsu-kyo full-moon bridge, the Tsuten-kyo, a miniature Oi-gawa and the rice field. 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:30; open every day except Dec 29–Jan 1. ¥300, ¥150 for over-65s.

Reopened 31 March 2026 after a four-year renewal into an immersive museum — the walk-in Nakamura-za playhouse, an enterable tenement room, the 26 m Nihonbashi span and the full-scale Hattori clock tower, and projection-mapped Edo-to-Tokyo galleries. 9:30–17:30, and to 19:30 on Saturdays; last admission 30 minutes before closing. Closed Mondays, or the following day when a Monday is a public holiday — the visit is Tue Nov 10, which is clear. ¥800 for the permanent exhibition; tickets are sold at the 1st-floor counter or online, and timed entry is not required.

The optional add-on at the end of the day — a strolling garden of famous named stones around the Daisensui pond, with the Ryotei pavilion standing over the water. Two Oedo-line stops east of Ryogoku. 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:30; open every day except Dec 29–Jan 1. ¥150, ¥70 for over-65s. About 40 minutes to walk the pond circuit.

address_jp: 〒636-0115 奈良県生駒郡斑鳩町法隆寺山内1-1
notes: The Western Precinct — the kondo and the five-storey pagoda — with the Daihozoin treasure galleries and the octagonal Yumedono of the Eastern Precinct. One ¥2,000 ticket covers all three precincts and is payable in cash only. Hours are 8:00–17:00 from 22 February to 3 November and 8:00–16:30 from 4 November to 21 February, with reception closing 30 minutes before; the Oct 29 visit falls in the earlier set. The Yumedono’s hidden Guze Kannon is unveiled each autumn from 22 October to 22 November, so it is on show on the day of the visit. About 20 minutes on foot from JR Horyuji Station, or the bus to Horyuji-sando. Allow 1.5–2 hours for the full precinct.

address_jp: 〒630-8563 奈良県奈良市西ノ京町457
notes: The East Pagoda is the only building standing from the temple’s foundation; the kondo, the West Pagoda and the Great Lecture Hall are 20th-century reconstructions of the Hakuho garan, funded by sutra-copying donations from 1968 onward. ¥1,000 admits to the Kondo, the Daikodo and the Toindo. Hours are 9:00–17:00 with reception to 16:30, as revised on 1 March 2024. One minute on foot from Kintetsu Nishinokyo Station. Allow about 1.5 hours.

The temple the Chinese monk Ganjin founded after his crossing to Japan: the kondo and its statuary, and the mausoleum grounds behind. ¥1,000 for the precinct, revised 1 April 2020; the Shin-Hozo treasure house is a separate ¥200. Hours are 8:30–17:00 with reception to 16:30. About 10 minutes on foot north of Yakushi-ji, on the same lane from Kintetsu Nishinokyo Station. Allow about an hour.

address_jp: 〒636-0123 奈良県生駒郡斑鳩町興留七丁目
notes: JR Yamatoji Line, the way in to Ikaruga from Kyoto or Nara. The temple is about 20 minutes on foot north of the station, or a short ride on the bus signed Horyuji-sando.

address_jp: 〒630-8563 奈良県奈良市六条一丁目
notes: Kintetsu Kashihara Line, one minute from Yakushi-ji’s south gate and about ten from Toshodai-ji. The way home on the Ikaruga day: coming from Kintetsu Kyoto, limited-express and express trains stop here in the hours from 10:00 to 16:59; outside that band the station is served by local trains.

address_jp: 〒632-0016 奈良県天理市川原城町
notes: One station complex shared by the JR Manyo Mahoroba (Sakurai) Line and the Kintetsu Tenri Line, and the northern trailhead of the Yamanobe-no-michi. Isonokami Jingu is about 40 minutes east on foot, straight up the Tenri Hondori arcade and over the Furu river. Convenience stores and supermarkets at the station; the walk has vending machines and a tea house on the line.

address_jp: 奈良県天理市布留町384
notes: The shrine that held the Yamato court’s weapons. National Treasures: the haiden, the haiden of the Izumo-Takeo subordinate shrine, and the seven-branched sword. Important Cultural Properties: the romon gate, the iron shields, the armour and the finds from the forbidden precinct. Free, no ticketing, no interior visit; long-tailed roosters roam the cedar approach. The gates are open roughly 5:30–17:30 and the exact times shift with the season, so the closing time here is approximate; the day arrives around 8:30, well inside the opening. About 40 minutes on foot east of Tenri Station.

address_jp: 奈良県天理市柳本町508
notes: The midpoint of the walk, founded in the 9th century. Its bell-tower gate is an Important Cultural Property of the Heian period, and the Amida triad in the main hall is another; the former Jizo-in beside it keeps a Japanese garden and a 400-year-old pine. From 23 October to the end of November the original 11-by-4-metre hell screen by Kano Sanraku is on show in the main hall in place of the replica shown the rest of the year, and the head priest reads it aloud at 1 pm on Saturdays and Sundays. On weekdays a reading is held only when a group has arranged one, and individual visitors may sit in on it, so on a weekday it is worth phoning ahead. 9:00–17:00, open every day of the year. ¥400 for adults; the grounds and halls take about 20 minutes to see, longer if the reading is running.

address_jp: 〒633-0082 奈良県桜井市茅原
notes: A subordinate shrine of Omiwa, on the trail about 40 minutes north of it. Known as Moto-Ise, a site where the Ise deity is said to have been enshrined before Ise itself. It has no honden and no hall: a torii stands in the open facing Mount Miwa, which is the object of worship. Free, open air, and walkable at any hour, so the times shown are all-day rather than gate hours. On 5 November its precinct holds the Toyosukiiri-hime annual rite at 11:00.

The southern end of the walk, and the oldest form of Shinto practice still in operation: there is no honden, because Mount Miwa behind the shrine is itself the deity. Worship at the precinct is unrestricted with no gate hours, which is why the times shown are all-day. The amulet office keeps 9:00–17:00, to 16:30 in winter, and the treasure hall opens only on the first of the month and on weekends and holidays, 9:30–15:30 with entry to 15:00, ¥300. The climb up Mount Miwa from Sai Shrine is suspended — the shrine posted the suspension in July 2026 with no resumption date, and it was still posted on 8 August. Five minutes on foot from the great torii to JR Miwa.

address_jp: 〒633-0061 奈良県桜井市三輪
notes: JR Manyo Mahoroba (Sakurai) Line, five minutes from Omiwa’s great torii and the end of the walk. About 25 minutes to Nara, roughly two trains an hour on weekdays and on Saturdays and holidays alike, with the last departure at 23:33 — the walk can therefore be ended late without risk. Four other stations sit on the route north of here, so any stage can be abandoned to a train within about twenty minutes.

A National Treasure of the Edo period, standing on the hillside above the Great Buddha Hall on a pillared platform that looks west over the whole Nara basin. It takes its name from the Shunie rite held here in the second month of the old calendar; fire broke out during the rite in 1667 and the present hall was rebuilt two years later, enlarged over the centuries to suit the ceremony it houses. The temple says the hall can be visited at any hour of the day or night, and its admission page charges only for the Great Buddha Hall, the Hokke-do, the Kaidan-do and the museum — so there is no gate and no fee here, which is why the times shown run right round the clock. A rite is held on the 18th of each month, from 8:00 April to October and 8:30 November to March, lasting about two hours; it can be heard from the west chamber if there is room. Tripods are not allowed on or around the terrace, and the temple asks for quiet at night. About 20 minutes — this is a viewing terrace, not a tour.

The oldest building at Todai-ji and a National Treasure of the Nara period, dated to the Tenpyo era from 733 and older than the temple itself — it was one of the main halls of Konshusen-ji, Todai-ji’s predecessor, and the Kegon sutra is said to have been expounded in Japan for the first time inside it. The rear sanctuary is the original; the front worship hall was rebuilt in 1199 by the monk Chogen. Ten Nara-period statues, all National Treasures, stand crowded together inside around the Fukukensaku Kannon that gave the hall its older name of Kensaku-do — among them the Kongo Rikishi pair, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the hidden Shukongojin, which is unveiled on 16 December only. The Nikko and Gakko figures that once flanked the main image now sit in the Todai-ji Museum for earthquake protection. 8:30–16:00 every day of the year, the same in both of the temple’s seasonal columns — ninety minutes before the Great Buddha Hall’s April-to-October close of 17:30, and the reason the upper precinct is done before mid afternoon. ¥800, cash only, charged separately from the Great Buddha Hall. About 20–30 minutes. A rite is held here on the 17th of each month, from 8:00 April to October, lasting about 50 minutes.

address_jp: 〒630-8213 奈良県奈良市登大路町50番地
price: ¥700 permanent galleries; Shoso-in Exhibition by advance timed ticket, price on the exhibition site
notes: The 78th Shoso-in Exhibition runs 24 October to 9 November 2026 with no closing day inside the run, 8:00–18:00 and to 20:00 on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays, last entry one hour before closing. Those are the times shown here, because the run covers most of the trip and the museum’s ordinary calendar would be the wrong badge for nearly all of it: outside the run it keeps 9:30–17:00, last entry 16:30, and closes on Mondays. The exhibition opens the imperial repository of Todai-ji once a year, and its 2026 ticketing was still unannounced on 8 August — the exhibition site says the ticket information comes in late August, and entry has been by dated and timed ticket bought in advance in recent years. The permanent Buddhist sculpture hall shows about a hundred statues from the Asuka to the Kamakura periods, National Treasures among them, and costs ¥700 for adults; the exhibition ticket also admits you to it. There is no visitor car park. Allow about 1.5–2 hours for the exhibition — an hour is enough only if it is empty, and it will not be.

address_jp: 〒630-8393 奈良県奈良市鵲町
notes: The merchant quarter that grew up on the precinct land of Gango-ji and developed from the Edo period through the Meiji, a few minutes south of Sarusawa Pond on the way back from the park. Lattice-fronted townhouses still line the lanes, many of them now cafes, craft shops and small museums, and red migawari-zaru monkey charms hang from the eaves. There is no gate and no opening time — it is a district of public streets, and every shop keeps its own hours. The Mochiidono arcade running into it calls itself, on its own site, the shopping street said to be the oldest in Nara. Landmarks inside it are Gango-ji, the Koshin-do hall, Goryo Shrine and the restored Naramachi Koshi-no-ie townhouse; the Naramachi south information centre Shika-no-Fune and the Naramachi Joho-kan can point you at the rest. It is where the Nara specialities are eaten — kakinoha-zushi, chagayu tea gruel, Yamato vegetables. Allow about an hour to an hour and a half as an evening descent that doubles as dinner.

address_jp: 〒630-8122 奈良県奈良市三条本町
notes: JR West — the Yamatoji, Nara and Manyo Mahoroba (Sakurai) lines. The Kyoto legs on this day are the Nara Line rapid, which arrives here and not at the Kintetsu station. Nara city loop buses to the park, Todai-ji and Kasuga leave from the east side. The Kintetsu station is a separate building about 1.1 km east, roughly a fifteen-minute walk along Sanjo-dori — the two are never interchangeable in a leg. No operator page could be cited: JR West publishes station pages only under undiscoverable ids, so the pin and the address are from OpenStreetMap and its Japanese reverse geocode.

address_jp: 〒606-0807 京都府京都市左京区下鴨泉川町59
notes: Twelve hectares of forest running south from Shimogamo Shrine's main hall to Kawai Shrine, and the shrine's own approach — the day walks north through it from the Kamo delta rather than arriving at the shrine gate. Kyoto City's register calls it plainly a historic site; the shrine gives it as a National Historic Site standing inside a precinct that holds two National Treasure main halls and 53 Important Cultural Property structures, and that precinct was inscribed as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in December 1994. The name is traced either to Tadasu-Tamayori-hime, the deity of Kawai Shrine, or to a tradition that the shrine's own deity judged the people's disputes here. Unfenced, free, no gate and no hours; a custom of standing in the stream that runs through it survives. The pin is the only one OpenStreetMap publishes for the wood and it coincides with the shrine's own node at the north end, so it points at the far end of the walk rather than the entrance.

address_jp: 〒606-0807 京都府京都市左京区下鴨泉川町59
notes: The principal auxiliary shrine of Shimogamo, standing in the Tadasu-no-Mori near its south end. Its deity is Tamayori-hime, mother of Emperor Jinmu, worshipped here as the deity of beauty because she was said to be as lovely as a jewel, and the shrine is a place of protection for women; its votive tablets are hand-mirror shaped and are made up with the visitor's own cosmetics. Kamo no Chomei, who wrote the Hojoki, was the son of this shrine's senior priest and spent his childhood here. Free. Its gate opens at 6:30 like the main shrine but closes at 16:30, half an hour before the inner precinct — the earlier of the two closings, and the one that binds a late arrival; the shrine notes that times can change for rites. The reconstruction of Chomei's ten-foot-square hut stands in the forest to the north of here, inside Shimogamo's paid area.

name_jp: 賀茂御祖神社（下鴨神社）
address_jp: 〒606-0807 京都府京都市左京区下鴨泉川町59
notes: One of the oldest shrines in Kyoto, the parent shrine of the Kamo pair and part of the 1994 World Heritage inscription, with a National Treasure main hall and the seven Kotosha zodiac sub-shrines. The times shown are the inner precinct inside the Romon gate; Kawai Shrine in the forest closes at 16:30, and the shrine says both can change for rites. No closed days and no admission to the precinct. The paid area — the Oidono, an Important Cultural Property that was the kitchen of the gods, the Mikurumayasha with its Aoi Matsuri material, the former Jingu-ji precinct holding the reconstruction of Kamo no Chomei's ten-foot-square hut, and the Shusuisha archive — is open 10:00-16:00 for ¥1,000, free for children of middle-school age and under. That fee is the shrine's own published figure and is twice the ¥500 this day was planned on, which came from third-party pages. Prayers are received 9:00-16:30 without booking. The day walks in from the south through Tadasu-no-Mori, then north up the river to Kamigamo on the Aoi Matsuri's own route and direction, parent shrine to child shrine.

name_jp: 賀茂別雷神社（上賀茂神社）
address_jp: 〒603-8047 京都府京都市北区上賀茂本山339
notes: The child shrine of the Kamo pair and the other half of the 1994 World Heritage inscription, with a National Treasure main hall and provisional hall and the two cones of raked sand before the Hosodono. The times shown are the second torii, which is the precinct proper; the Romon gate and the amulet office keep 8:00-16:45, and prayers are received 9:00-16:00. The precinct is free and open every day; the main hall and provisional hall are National Treasures and 41 further structures are Important Cultural Properties. The priest-guided visit into the inner court — an explanation of the Kamo myth in the Naoraiden, the Takakuradono treasure display, and standing in front of the National Treasure halls themselves — is received 10:00-16:00 for ¥500 a head; photography and eating are not allowed inside. Two cautions from the shrine itself: the visit is suspended or its hours changed for rites, and it is not run at all during special campaign periods, when a different and usually dearer opening replaces it. The autumn 2026 programme was not announced when this was checked; the autumn entry still on the shrine's page is the 2025 one. Ota Shrine, five minutes away, holds its autumn rite on 10 November. Buses 4 and 46 stop at the shrine gate, 9 and 37 five minutes away, and Kitaoji or Kitayama subway is 25 minutes on foot.

address_jp: 京都府京都市北区上賀茂藤ノ木町・上賀茂池殿町辺り
notes: The lane of the shrine's own priestly families, following the Myojin-gawa as it leaves the Kamigamo precinct — earthen bridges, earthen walls, gates and front gardens, and the inokosasu gable member that is particular to these houses. It grew as a priests' quarter from the Muromachi period and is a nationally selected Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, chosen in 1988. Free, exterior viewing, about 500 m of lane, two minutes from the shrine gate. The Nishimura house is the only residence open to the public and its season for 2026 is not published, so it is not counted on. Kyoto City gives the district's address as around Kamigamo Fujinoki-cho and Kamigamo Ikedono-cho, and publishes no hours for it; the pin is the first of those two townships.

address_jp: 京都府京都市下京区烏丸通塩小路下ル東塩小路町
notes: The hinge of the Kansai half of the trip: the Nozomi from Tokyo arrives here on Wed 28 Oct, the hotel is a few minutes away on the north side, and the Takao, Daigo, Yoshino and Uji days all begin and end in this building. JR West gives the ticket counters as Midori-no-madoguchi 06:30-21:00 and the ticket machines 05:30-23:00, with operator support at the machines 08:00-20:00; the Central, West and Underground East gates run from 04:35 to the last train, and the Hachijo East gate 06:50-23:00. ICOCA and the other IC cards work at every gate, and there are coin lockers and a station rent-a-car desk. Two of the Kansai dinners are placed on the department-store restaurant floor in the station building rather than out on the day, because the mountains close early. JR West prints the street address without a postal code, so none is shipped.

address_jp: 京都府京都市右京区嵯峨天竜寺車道町11番地1
notes: JR Sagano (San'in) Line — the start of the Takao day, which walks out of the city from here rather than riding to the temples. There is no staffed ticket window; the ticket machine with operator support runs 05:30-23:00 (operator 08:00-20:00), the gate is open from first to last train with staff present 06:30-19:30 and 23:00 to the last train and an intercom at all other times. ICOCA works, and there are coin lockers. This is the JR station: the Randen tram terminus and the Hankyu station of similar name are separate buildings about a kilometre away, and no leg of this trip uses them. The walking route to Kiyotaki leaves the town through Toriimoto and crosses the old Kokoromi-toge pass road, which is the course Hankyu publishes through this valley.

address_jp: 京都府京都市右京区嵯峨鳥居本仙翁町・嵯峨鳥居本六反町辺り
notes: The approach town to Atago-jinja, the fire-prevention shrine on the mountain above, which grew as both a temple-gate town and a farming village and kept the two characters side by side: machiya-style townhouses with mushiko lattice windows next to thatched farmhouses of the kind called kuzuya. The Agency for Cultural Affairs lists it as an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings, type gate-town, nationally selected on 21 May 1979, area 2.6 hectares — one of Kyoto's four such districts. It is an open street with no gate and no admission. The city runs a free preservation hall in the district (Kyoto City Saga Toriimoto Machinami Hall, Senno-cho 8, 075-864-2406) in a house built in the early Meiji period, open 10:00-16:00, closed Mondays — the following day when a Monday is a public holiday — and 26 December to 6 January; you pass through here well before it opens, so the day does not count on it.

address_jp: 京都府京都市右京区嵯峨清滝深谷町
notes: A hamlet at the south-east foot of Atago-yama that grew up as the lodging stage on the pilgrimage to the mountain shrine, on the Kiyotaki river where the Watarizaru and Kinrei bridges cross. Kyoto City's own marker gives the river's two gorges their names: upstream of here, towards Takao, is the Kin'unkei, and downstream the Kinreikei. The Kin'unkei walk between here and Takao-bashi is the middle of the Takao day — about 3 km and roughly two hours, described by the Kyoto City Transportation Bureau's own course as having little elevation change and being walkable by beginners, with a warning that the rock underfoot is slippery after rain; it is also part of the Kyoto Isshu Trail's Kitayama-West section. There is no toilet anywhere between Takao-bashi and Kiyotaki. Coming in from Saga-Arashiyama on foot, the published walking course crosses the old Kokoromi-toge road over the top rather than following the road through the Kiyotaki tunnel. The pin is the Kiyotaki bus stop in the middle of the hamlet.

address_jp: 〒616-8292 京都府京都市右京区梅ヶ畑高雄町5番地
notes: The main stop on the Takao day, reached by about 350 stone steps up from the Takao-bashi bridge. Founded in 781 as the clan temple of the Wake family; Kukai lived here for fourteen years from 809 and built the ground of the Shingon school on it, and Mongaku revived it at the end of the Heian period. The temple gives its precinct hours as 09:00-16:00 with no closing day, one figure with no seasonal variant anywhere on its site, and admission as 1,000 yen for adults, a rate in force since 1 July 2024. The National Treasure Yakushi Nyorai stands in the Kondo and is on view at all times; the National Treasure bell, one of the three famous bells of Japan, is never shown, and the National Treasure portraits of Minamoto no Yoritomo and Taira no Shigemori are put out only from 1 to 5 May. The kawarake-nage — throwing unglazed clay discs off the Jizo-in terrace over the Kin'unkei gorge — starts here. Two special openings are relevant to the dates: the National Treasure Five Great Kokuzo Bosatsu in the pagoda are shown 10-12 October 2026, before this trip arrives, and the Daishi-do, an Important Cultural Property building holding the Important Cultural Property carved-wood image of Kobo Daishi, is opened 1-7 November, 09:00-16:00, for 500 yen on top of admission. The temple prints those November dates without a year, so the 2026 repeat is confirmed close to the trip rather than assumed.

address_jp: 〒616-8291 京都府京都市右京区梅ヶ畑槇尾町1
notes: The middle temple of the three Takao valley temples, reached over the vermilion Shigetsu bridge and a short stone stair. Founded in the Tencho era, 824 to 834, by Chisen, a senior disciple of Kukai, as a branch temple of Jingo-ji; revived in the 1270s, granted the title Byodoshin-oin by the retired emperor Go-Uda in 1290 and independent from Jingo-ji thereafter; burnt in the Eiroku era and rebuilt in 1602 by Myonin. The present main hall is the 1700 rebuilding paid for by Keishoin, mother of the fifth Tokugawa shogun. Inside are the main image, a standing Shakyamuni of the Seiryo-ji type attributed to Unkei, together with a Heian-period thousand-armed Kannon and a Kamakura-period Aizen Myoo, and a moss garden seen from within the hall; a koyamaki cedar in the grounds is held to be seven hundred years old and to have given the hill its name. The temple publishes its hours, 09:00-17:00, and no closing day; the temple publishes no admission figure on any of its pages, so the one here is the Kyoto Prefecture tourism federation's, which gives free entry to the grounds and 700 yen for the hall, and also records that the guest hall is specially opened from late October to the end of November — a period that covers this visit.

address_jp: 〒616-8295 京都府京都市右京区梅ヶ畑栂尾町8
notes: The last stop of the Takao day and a component of the World Heritage site Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto. The temple's own account: an old foundation, later a branch of Jingo-ji, given to Myoe in 1206 by the retired emperor Go-Toba, who restored it under the name it now carries. The National Treasure it admits you to is the Sekisui-in, Myoe's own residential hall and a landmark of Japanese domestic architecture; the temple also holds the four Choju Jinbutsu Giga scrolls, National Treasures of the late Heian and Kamakura periods, whose authorship it states plainly is unknown despite the traditional attribution to Toba Sojo Kakuyu. The tea garden in the grounds carries a stone reading "Japan's oldest tea garden", but the temple's own tea page states that the oldest garden was across the Kiyotaki river at Fukaize Sanbongi and that this plot is thought to be the site of Jumujin-in, a central monastic hall; the temple deflates its own monument. Admission is 1,000 yen for the Sekisui-in with a further 500 yen mountain-entry fee in the autumn period, whose dates the temple does not publish; opening is 08:30-17:00. The large-scale repair of the typhoon damage of September 2018 — the Kondo, the founder's hall, the stone walls and the main approach — was completed on 31 March 2020 on the temple's own notice, so the precinct is open; a page elsewhere that still says only the Sekisui-in can be visited is describing the years before it. The temple posts notices on its own site, which is worth a look again close to the trip.

address_jp: 京都府京都市右京区梅ケ畑殿畑町
notes: Where the Takao day leaves the valley, three minutes from Kozan-ji's gate. Two operators use it: Kyoto City Bus route 8, which starts from Shijo Karasuma and ends here — the transport bureau's own route page names Takao and Toganoo as the outer terminus, so buses begin their run empty at this stop — and West Japan JR Bus's Takao-Keihoku line, which runs through to the terminal in front of Kyoto Station. Both run late into the evening and the weekday, Saturday and holiday timetables are the same; the departures the day actually uses are in the day's own legs. The street address is OpenStreetMap's, since neither operator publishes one for the stop.

address_jp: 〒601-1325 京都府京都市伏見区醍醐東大路町22
notes: The lower precinct of a Shingon mountain temple of the World Heritage list. The temple dates its beginning to the early Heian period, when Shobo Rigen Daishi consecrated his own carvings of Juntei and Nyoirin Kannon and set the first mark of its founding on the upper mountain; the halls below came afterwards, under the patronage of Emperor Daigo and Empress Onshi. The temple divides itself into three ticketed areas — Sanbo-in, the Garan and the Reihokan treasure house — and sells them as one ticket for 1,500 yen, any two for 1,000, or any one for 600; all of them are bought at the Sanbo-in reception rather than at separate gates. The pin is on the Garan itself, east of the Sanbo-in gate where the ticket is bought. Two National Treasures stand here: the Kondo, first raised by decree of Emperor Daigo in 926 and rebuilt under Hideyoshi and Hideyori with a hall moved from Yuasa in Kishu, and the five-storey pagoda, begun in 936 and completed in 951, whose first storey carries the mandalas and the eight Shingon patriarchs that are a source of Japanese esoteric painting. The Nio figures in the west great gate are an Important Cultural Property of 1134. Precinct hours run 09:00 to 17:00 from 1 March to the first Sunday of December — 6 December in 2026 — and 09:00 to 16:30 through the winter, with the reception closing thirty minutes before the gates. The Reihokan holds three exhibition rooms, and the temple states that one of them is open the whole year round, closed only for the first three days of January and for occasional special closures. Admission takes cash, credit cards and electronic money.

address_jp: 〒601-1325 京都府京都市伏見区醍醐東大路町22
price: Part of the Daigo-ji ticket: ¥1,500 all three areas / ¥1,000 any two / ¥600 any one (palace special viewing +¥500)
notes: The abbots’ residence of Daigo-ji, founded in 1115 by Shokaku, the temple’s fourteenth head, and the first thing inside the main gate; this is also where every Daigo-ji ticket is sold, so it is the practical entrance to the whole precinct. Most of its buildings are Important Cultural Properties. Two are National Treasures: the Omote-shoin, which faces the garden and carries a balustraded veranda with a spring pavilion at its south-west corner in the manner of Heian shinden architecture, with sliding-door paintings of willows and of hill-and-field landscapes in its upper and middle rooms attributed to the Hasegawa Tohaku school, peacocks and cycads by Ishida Yutei in the lower room, and a lower-room floor whose mats lift away to reveal a Noh stage; and the Kara-mon, the gate opened only for imperial messengers, originally black lacquer with gold leaf on its four large chrysanthemum and paulownia crests, and restored to that state over about eighteen months in July 2010. The garden is designated both a Special Historic Site and a Special Place of Scenic Beauty; Hideyoshi drew its basic design himself in 1598 for the Daigo flower-viewing party, and the Fujito-ishi standing in it had passed through the hands of successive warlords before him. A special viewing of the palace rooms costs 500 yen beyond the admission ticket. Hours and reception follow the temple as a whole.

address_jp: 〒601-1325 京都府京都市伏見区醍醐東大路町22
notes: CLOSED AT THE TIME OF WRITING — CHECK THE TEMPLE’S FRONT PAGE BEFORE SETTING OUT. Daigo-ji’s own front page carries the notice that, because of a danger of landslides on part of the mountain path, entry to Kami-Daigo is prohibited for the time being. That notice has been carried continuously since at least late June 2026, its wording hardening from a weather warning, to a pending safety inspection of the approach, to the present landslide wording. The standing schedule below is still published underneath it, so the schedule is not evidence that the mountain is open; only a fresh reading of the front page is. This is where Daigo-ji began: the ninth-century original of the temple, holding the National Treasure Yakushi-do and the National Treasure haiden of Kiyotaki-gu, the Nyoirin-do and the Kaisan-do — both Important Cultural Properties — and the Daigo spring, which Shobo is said to have found by spiritual power at the retreat he built here and whose water can still be drunk. The Kaisan-do, rebuilt by Toyotomi Hideyori in 1606, is in the temple's words the largest hall on the mountain. The pin is on the Yakushi-do at the summit precinct, not on the trailhead. Access, when it is open, is on foot only and only from the Nyonin-do trailhead below, where climbers write themselves into an entry register; the temple gives the climb as about an hour each way and says a visit including the halls needs at least three hours. Registration is open 09:00 to 15:00 from 1 March to the first Sunday of December and 09:00 to 14:00 in winter, and the temple instructs climbers to be back down at the foot by 17:00. Entry can also be refused for weather. No separate fee for the mountain is published anywhere on the temple’s site. The halls are seen mainly from the outside.

address_jp: 京都府京都市伏見区醍醐高畑町
notes: Kyoto Municipal Subway, Tozai Line — the rail end of the Daigo-ji day. First and last trains towards Uzumasa-Tenjingawa run at 05:19 and 23:32, and towards Rokujizo at 05:49 and 24:15. There are lifts from street level to the concourse at exit 1 on the west side of the ring road, at the Paseo Daigoro east building on the east side, and behind the bicycle park; the lift to the platform is straight ahead through the ticket gates. Toilets are available only within operating hours. The street address is OpenStreetMap’s, since the transport bureau publishes no address for the station.

address_jp: 京都府京都市山科区安朱北屋敷町
notes: The interchange on the way to Daigo-ji, used in both roles on the same day: arrive on JR from Kyoto, change to the Tozai subway, and reverse it coming home. Three separate stations share the name — JR West’s, the municipal subway’s and Keihan’s — and they are kept as one record here; the coordinates and address are JR West’s, whose own station page gives Anshu Kitayashiki-cho and prints no postcode. On the JR side there is a ticket office open 08:00 to 20:00, Midori ticket machines from 05:00 to 23:00 and Midori Plus machines from 05:30 to 23:00 with operator assistance 08:00 to 20:00; the gates are open from 04:30 to the last train, ICOCA is accepted, and both EX and 5489 reserved tickets can be collected. On the subway side, first and last trains run at 05:27 and 23:41 towards Uzumasa-Tenjingawa and at 05:40 and 24:07 towards Rokujizo, and the station telephone is 075-595-2750. The Tozai line does not reach Kyoto Station, which is why the day changes here.

address_jp: 〒611-0021 京都府宇治市宇治蓮華116
price: ¥700 (garden + Hoshokan museum; no garden-only ticket) · Phoenix Hall interior ¥300
notes: The World Heritage temple on the Uji river, and the building on the ten-yen coin. The hours held here are the garden gate — 08:45 to 17:30, reception closing at 17:15, open every day of the year; the other windows inside it run to their own clocks. The Byodo-in Museum Hoshokan, where the temple’s National Treasures are displayed, is open 09:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:45 and is also open year-round, and the museum shop keeps the same hours. Admission of 700 yen covers the garden and the museum together; there is no garden-only price. The interior of the Phoenix Hall is separate: 300 yen, given as an offering, with parties of fifty leaving every twenty minutes between 09:30 and 16:10. It cannot be booked in advance — reception opens at 09:10 at the interior-viewing desk inside the garden and runs first-come until the slots are gone, which can be well before the last departure, and services and ceremonies occasionally suspend it altogether. A change to interior viewing ran from 16 June to 15 October 2026 and ends before this trip. The Saho Fuka teahouse opens 10:00 to 16:30 with last orders at 16:00 and closes Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday unless the day is a public holiday, and the stamp desk is open 09:10 to 17:00. Two standing notices affect what is seen: at busy times the museum may close its video room and its excavated-objects corner, which the temple handles flexibly and which leaves the National Treasure displays untouched; and the Kannon-do, an Important Cultural Property of the mid-Kamakura period under its first major repair since 1922, stays behind a 1.8 m construction barricade that cannot be approached, with reconsecration expected in spring 2027 or later. The restrictions on the Ogi-no-shiba lawn and on the paths north and east of the wisteria trellis were lifted in January 2026.

address_jp: 〒611-0021 京都府宇治市宇治山田59
notes: A World Heritage shrine across the river from Byodo-in, and the second of Uji’s two listings. Its honden is a National Treasure and the oldest surviving shrine building in Japan: three Heian-period sanctuaries in the ichigensha-nagare style under one roof, the outer two large and the middle one small. The haiden, also a National Treasure, is a residential building in the shinden manner, said to be a remnant of the Uji detached palace. The shrine enshrines Uji-no-Wakiiratsuko with Emperors Ojin and Nintoku; by its own telling, Uji-no-Wakiiratsuko was Ojin’s youngest son and named heir, spent three years refusing the throne in favour of his elder brother Nintoku, and took his own life to end the deadlock, and the shrine grew from his burial. It was once one body with the Uji-jinja below it, and is called the tutelary shrine of Byodo-in. The grounds are free. Hours of 09:00 to 16:20 with last entry at 16:10 are published by the Kyoto Prefecture tourism federation, not by the shrine, whose own site states only that amulets, fortunes and goshuin are given out from 09:00 and not before, however early the staff are in the office. Payment at the shrine is cash only — no cards and no QR codes.

address_jp: 〒611-0011 京都府宇治市五ケ庄三番割34
notes: Head temple of Obaku, the third of the Japanese Zen schools alongside Rinzai and Soto, one stop north of Uji. It was founded in 1661 by the Chinese monk Ingen Ryuki, who had been abbot of the Obakusan Manpukuji in Fuqing, Fujian, and who came to Japan in 1654 at the age of 63 with twenty disciples; he named this temple after his own. The school called itself a branch of Rinzai until it was recognised separately in 1876. What makes the place unlike any other temple in Japan is that it was built in the late-Ming Chinese manner and has kept it: the main halls stand on a single axis with matching buildings mirrored left and right, and the details are Chinese throughout — swastika-pattern balustrades, round windows, peach-shaped ornaments carved on the doors, and the arched ceiling known as the Obaku ceiling. The paths are paved with square stones set as diamonds between stone rails, in imitation of a dragon’s scales. Three halls are National Treasures on the temple’s own reckoning: the Daiyu-hoden, the main hall and the largest building, and the only historic structure in Japan built of teak; the Tenno-den at the entrance, holding the four heavenly kings with Maitreya and Skanda; and the Hatto. Twenty-three main buildings, the corridors and the tablets are Important Cultural Properties. The sutras are still chanted in a Chinese reading. Hours are 09:00 to 17:00 with reception closing at 16:30; the stamp office also closes at 16:30 and the shop at 16:00, admission is 500 yen, and the temple gives a visit as thirty minutes to an hour. There is no fixed weekly closing day, but the prefecture’s listing records closures as irregular. Fucha-ryori, the Chinese Buddhist vegetarian meal Ingen brought with him, is served 11:30 to 14:30 with seating by 13:00 and must be reserved three days ahead.

address_jp: 京都府宇治市宇治宇文字16番地
notes: JR West, Nara Line — the Uji day arrives and leaves here. This is the JR station, not the Keihan station of the same name, which stands on the far bank. There is a ticket office open 08:00 to 20:00 and Midori ticket machines from 05:00 to 23:00; the gates are open from the first train to the last, ICOCA is accepted, and both EX and 5489 reserved tickets can be collected here. No postcode is printed on the operator’s station page.

address_jp: 京都府宇治市五ケ庄新開18番地
notes: JR West, Nara Line — one stop north of Uji, and the stop for Manpuku-ji. There is no ticket office and no Midori machine; a commuter-pass machine runs 05:00 to 23:50, and the gates are open from the first train to the last, with ICOCA accepted and an intercom to staff. Station staff are present only in stretches: 06:40 to 12:20, 13:20 to 14:30, 16:30 to 18:00, 19:00 to 22:00, and 22:40 to the last train. Reserved tickets bought through EX or 5489 cannot be collected here. No postcode is printed on the operator’s station page.

address_jp: 奈良県吉野郡吉野町丹治
notes: Kintetsu’s station at the foot of the mountain. The street address here is OpenStreetMap’s locality, not a figure printed by the railway — Kintetsu’s own station page does not publish one. Three ways go up to the village, and which of them is running depends on the day of the week, which is the fact that decides how you get up. The ropeway from Senbonguchi to Yoshinoyama runs Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday only, from 09:20 to 17:20, four cars an hour at five, twenty, thirty-five and fifty past. On Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday it does not run at all and a substitute micro-bus runs instead, up at 09:35, 10:35, 11:05, 11:40, 12:05, 13:35, 14:35, 15:35 and 16:05, and down at 09:50, 10:50, 11:20, 11:55, 12:20, 13:50, 14:50, 15:50 and 16:20. The last descent by substitute bus is therefore an hour earlier than the ropeway’s, and there is a gap between the 12:20 and the 13:50. Public holidays follow the day of the week they fall on, so a holiday on a Tuesday still gets the bus and not the ropeway. The bus fare is 500 yen one way for an adult and 250 yen for a child, cash only, paid in the vehicle, and the operator asks for coins; hand baggage is 250 yen, counted from about 20 by 20 by 50 centimetres or a cabin case from size S upward, while pushchairs and wheelchairs are free. The ropeway is 500 yen one way and 900 yen return. If a bus is full the operator’s own instruction is to wait for the next one or to walk up the Nanamagari path, which is the third way up and needs no service at all. Higher up, the Oku-senbon route bus between Yoshino-jingu and Oku-senbon-guchi runs at weekends only: never on a weekday and never on a public holiday, unless that holiday falls on a Sunday. It is also suspended each winter from the second Monday of December to the first Friday of March.

address_jp: 〒639-3115 奈良県吉野郡吉野町吉野山2498
notes: The head temple of Kinpusen Shugen Honshu and the centre of Shugendo, the mountain religion founded by En no Gyoja. Its main hall, the Zao-do, is a National Treasure and a core asset of the World Heritage listing made in 2004 for the sacred sites and pilgrimage routes of the Kii mountain range. The temple gives its height as 34 metres and its skirt roof as 36 metres on each side, and states that among Japan’s ancient wooden buildings it is second in size only to the Great Buddha Hall of Todai-ji. The present hall was rebuilt in 1592 after repeated fires, the last of them in 1586. Inside stands what the temple's own about page calls the largest shrine cabinet in the country, holding the three Kongo Zao Gongen, hidden images of which the central one is over seven metres tall. The three are being shown for the autumn special opening from 24 October to 30 November 2026, daily from 08:30 to 16:00, and the hours and price given here are that opening’s: 1,600 yen for an adult, 1,200 for a middle or high school student, 800 for a primary school child. Outside the opening the same hall keeps the same 08:30 to 16:00 hours and costs 800 yen for an adult, 600 and 400 for students and children. Entry may be restricted for a time during services. The temple states that the purpose of the opening is to raise funds for the repair of the Niomon, and a concurrent exhibition of paintings by Matsuda Daiji is held in the Okuden Honji-do. The morning service at 06:30 and the evening service at 16:30 may be attended, free outside the special opening period and included in the admission during it. The Niomon, the temple’s other National Treasure and its oldest building, is under a full dismantling repair and cannot be seen. It is 20.3 metres high on a castle-like stone base, its lower storey dating from the Nanbokucho period and its upper from the Kosho era, and it faces north to receive pilgrims entering the mountains from that side while the main hall faces south. The work is being run directly by Nara Prefecture’s cultural properties conservation office, which has a branch site at the temple; it began in the 2020 financial year and is aimed at completion in the 2028 financial year, after the survey found the foundations sinking on the east side and insect damage and rot in the timbers. The previous dismantling repair ran from 1943 to 1950. The two Nio statues that stand in it, 5.3 metres tall and second in size only to those of Todai-ji’s Nandaimon, were carved by the Nanto sculptor Kojo in the Engen era, and are on deposit at the Nara National Museum for the duration of the works — where they can be seen only until 13 September 2026, because that museum’s sculpture hall then closes until about spring 2028. In the window of this trip they are visible in neither place. Elsewhere in the precinct are the Kane-no-torii, an Important Cultural Property about 200 metres north of the Niomon, the first of the four gates on the way to the peaks and said by tradition to have been cast from the copper left over from the Great Buddha of Todai-ji; the Nancho Myoho-den, a three-storey pagoda of 1958 standing where Emperor Go-Daigo kept his palace; and the Shihonzakura, four cherry trees marking where Prince Morinaga held his last banquet in 1333.

address_jp: 〒639-3115 奈良県吉野郡吉野町吉野山579
notes: A World Heritage site and, on the shrine's own account, the only surviving temporary palace of the Southern Court. It began as Yoshimizu-in, a high-ranking Shugendo monks’ lodging founded by En no Gyoja more than 1,300 years ago, and became a shrine in 1875 at the separation of Buddhism and Shinto, taking its present form because Emperor Go-Daigo had made it his palace. It enshrines Go-Daigo, Kusunoki Masashige and Yoshimizu Soshin Hoin. Three histories run through the same rooms: in 1185 Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Shizuka Gozen and Benkei hid here, and the room in which they spent their last time together survives with the weapons and clothing Yoshitsune left behind; in 1336 Go-Daigo made the building his palace, beginning the fifty-seven years and four emperors of the Southern Court; and in 1594 Toyotomi Hideyoshi used it as the headquarters of his flower-viewing party, staying about five days with Tokugawa Ieyasu, Kato Kiyomasa, Maeda Toshiie, Date Masamune and a train of five thousand, holding poetry, tea and Noh gatherings and leaving behind the Noh masks and gold screens — one painted by Kano Sansetsu, one by Kano Eitoku — that are shown in the shoin today. The shoin itself is the point of the visit: an Important Cultural Property that the shrine describes as the oldest surviving example of shoin-style residential architecture in Japan and the first page of that history, with an unusually wide and shallow alcove, staggered shelves supported without a strut, chamfered pillars whose broad chamfers date them, nail covers made of wood rather than metal, and adzed ceiling boards. The gate opens at 09:00 and closes at 17:00; the shoin itself is open 09:00 to 16:30, and the amulet and seal desk also closes at 16:30. Admission is 600 yen for an adult, 400 for a middle or high school student and 300 for a primary school child. From the precinct beside the car park is the view called Hitome Senbon, a thousand cherries at a glance, taking in the Naka-senbon and Kami-senbon slopes; it is also called Hitome Junen, on the belief that one look adds ten years to a life. The shrine publishes no telephone number and asks that enquiries be made through the contact form on its site.

address_jp: 〒639-3115 奈良県吉野郡吉野町吉野山1612
notes: A World Heritage site in the Kami-senbon: an intact Momoyama compound of main hall, offering hall, worship hall, tower gate and cloister, all designated Important Cultural Properties together, with the three shrines of the honden built as one roofed range. The buildings were rebuilt in 1604 by Toyotomi Hideyori, who was born after his father prayed here for a child, which is why the shrine is also called Komori-no-miya and is trusted for conception, safe birth and the protection of children. The chief deity is Ame-no-mikumari-no-okami, who governs the dividing of water. The seated image of Tamayori-hime among the six other deities is a National Treasure and is not shown; a seated image of Ame-no-yorozu-takuhata-chihata-hime is an Important Cultural Property and is likewise not shown. The precinct is free. Hours are 08:00 to 16:00 with no closing day, extended to 17:00 in April only. These hours and this address are the Yoshinoyama Tourist Association’s and the Nara Prefecture tourism board’s, which agree exactly; the shrine has no site of its own, and the association’s listing records that in its own homepage field. No telephone number ships because the two channels give different ones — the association gives 0746-32-2717 at Onamochi Shrine, the prefecture gives 0746-32-3012 at the chief priest’s house — and neither is published by this shrine itself. There is a free car park with room for two or three cars.

address_jp: 〒639-3115 奈良県吉野郡吉野町吉野山1651
notes: A World Heritage site standing quietly in the Oku-senbon, the top segment of the village road. It is an ancient shrine listed in the Engishiki as a major shrine, and it enshrines Kanayamahiko-no-kami, the tutelary deity of Kinpusen — the whole range from Yoshino to Sanjogatake — worshipped both as a god who keeps living things from withering and, as lord of a mountain of gold ore, as a god of gold. From the medieval period it has been known as a training place of Shugendo. Its worship hall was moved here from the old Yoshino-jingu. A little below the shrine buildings stands the tower where Minamoto no Yoshitsune is said to have hidden from his pursuers; when they surrounded it he is said to have kicked his way out through the roof, which is why it is also called the kicked-through tower. Access is free and unrestricted: the tourism listing carries an opening-hours field and fills it with the words for free worship at any time, so the times shown here are all-day rather than gate hours. There is no car park and no site of its own; the same listing records that in its homepage field. No telephone number ships because the two channels that carry this shrine give different ones — the Yoshinoyama Tourist Association gives 0746-32-2717 at Onamochi Shrine, the Nara Prefecture tourism board gives 0746-32-3012 at the chief priest’s house.

The full-day alternative to the Yoshino ridge if that day is rained off: shorter, largely covered, and reached from the same Kintetsu Minami-Osaka line, fifteen minutes on foot from Taimadera Station. The temple states that it is the only place in the country where both ancient pagodas survive. The East Pagoda, of the Nara period, is the oldest building on the site, and the West Pagoda followed a little later, into the early Heian period; both are three-storeyed and both are National Treasures. The main hall, the Mandara-do, is also a National Treasure, its inner sanctuary keeping the Tenpyo form while the outer part was extended at the end of the Heian period; it holds the Taima Mandala in a National Treasure cabinet of the Tenpyo period, standing on a National Treasure dais given by Minamoto no Yoritomo. The mandala shown today is the Bunki copy, an Important Cultural Property; the legend is that Princess Chujo wove the original in a single night after copying a thousand scrolls of a sutra. The Kondo, an Important Cultural Property rebuilt in the Kamakura period, holds the temple’s original object of worship, a seated Miroku of the Hakuho period that is a National Treasure and the oldest clay statue in Japan, guarded by four heavenly kings of which three are the oldest dry-lacquer statues in Japan. The Kodo, also Kamakura and also an Important Cultural Property, holds a range of Heian and Kamakura sculpture. The bronze bell near the Niomon was cast in the 680s and is the oldest in Japan, older than the dated bell at Myoshin-ji, and is a National Treasure; the stone lantern in front of the Kondo, cut from Nijo-san tuff, is the oldest in Japan and an Important Cultural Property. The three main halls are open 09:00 to 17:00 and cost 1,000 yen for an adult and 500 for a primary school child, with reception at the main hall itself. The precinct may be walked freely between the same hours. Nakanobo, the temple’s oldest sub-temple and the place where Princess Chujo took the tonsure, is a separate 500 yen and is open the same hours; it holds the Kogaen garden, which is both a historic site and a place of scenic beauty, a tea room with a great round window that is an Important Cultural Property, and a treasure hall whose displays are changed through the year. A surcharge is added to the Nakanobo ticket during its own special display periods, which are announced year by year. Other sub-temples open at their own discretion: Sainan-in with an Edo garden, Gonen-in with peonies, and Okunoin, which keeps Honen and a treasure house of Pure Land material.

address_jp: 広島市中区中島町1及び大手町1-10
notes: The park is free and open at all times, with no closing day. It covers 122,100 square metres; construction began in 1950, it was substantially finished around August 1955 and opened to use on 1 April 1956. About 1,500 tall trees stand in it, some 300 of them cherries, and 35 memorials and monuments are set within it. The Memorial Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims carries the inscription “Rest in peace, for the error shall not be repeated”, and the register of the names of the dead is kept in the stone chamber at its centre. The Flame of Peace was designed by Tange Kenzo, its pedestal an abstraction of two hands opened upward, and it is to burn on until the day nuclear weapons vanish from the earth. The Children’s Peace Monument was raised for Sasaki Sadako, who died of leukaemia, and for the other children killed by the bomb; it stands nine metres high, with a bronze girl at its top holding up a golden folded crane. The Peace Bell is embossed with a map of a world without borders, for “the world is one”. The Monument in Memory of the Korean Victims stands on a turtle-shaped pedestal beneath a crown carved with twin dragons, and its move into the park was completed on 21 July 1999. The Atomic Bomb Memorial Mound holds the ashes of about 70,000 victims inside its earthen mound, and a memorial service is held there each 6 August. Counting the wider area around it, 209 atomic-bomb-related memorials stand in and around the park.

address_jp: 広島市中区大手町一丁目10番
notes: Free and outdoors. The building was the Hiroshima Prefectural Products Exhibition Hall, designed by the Czech architect Jan Letzel and completed in 1915; its distinctive green dome made it a landmark to the city before the bombing. It stood about 160 metres from the hypocentre, was destroyed in an instant on 6 August 1945, and everyone inside was killed. Its registration as a World Heritage site was decided at the World Heritage Committee held in Mexico in December 1996, after Japan widened the criteria for designating historic sites to cover sites down to the end of the Second World War and formally designated it a historic site in June 1995. On 18 September 2025 it was designated a Special Historic Site, the first site of the Meiji period or later in Japan to be given that rank, the city stating that its value was newly and highly assessed as a monument that conveys the disaster of the bombing and continues to argue for the abolition of nuclear weapons and a lasting world peace. Five major preservation projects have been carried out since 1967, the most recent in 2020 and 2021, covering crack repair, reinforcement, waterproofing and seismic work, and its soundness is surveyed every three years.

Confidence stays medium while the two figures disagree.

address_jp: 〒636-0116 奈良県生駒郡斑鳩町法隆寺2丁目2-35
notes: The retirement house of Kitabatake Harufusa, a bakumatsu loyalist who became a judicial official under Meiji, built about a hundred and thirty years ago; the tablet reading Fukokuen that hangs in the main house was brushed by Prince Arisugawa, with whom the household was on close terms. From 1954 it served as Ikaruga's municipal wedding hall, and it is now a cafe furnished in Yoshino timber and Akahada ware. It stands about 270 metres south-east of the Yumedono, which is where a Horyuji visit ends, and roughly 400 metres east of the two gate-street restaurants; Tabelog measures it 1,230 metres from the station against Matsumotoya's 1,205, so the walk out to the train is the same length whichever of them you eat at. Thirty-nine seats, a private room for eight, non-smoking, and a garden that people wait in. Credit cards, electronic money and QR payment are all accepted and an English menu exists, both of which are unusual on this street. The kitchen's own booking slots are 11:00, 11:30, 13:00 and 13:30 and there is no slot in the twelve o'clock hour at all, which is also the only hour anyone reports waiting to be seated. Two official town bodies publish different closing days for it, the Horyuji information centre saying Wednesdays only and the Waikaru tourism office saying Tuesdays and Wednesdays; the shop's own site and Tabelog both say Wednesdays, and the shop's site is actively maintained, so Wednesdays is what this record carries. The Wednesday closure is carried structurally in the hours rather than as a closing note, because a closing note suppresses the live open-now badge and this shop's schedule is not in fact uncertain; the two riders that a note would have held are that a Wednesday falling on a public holiday is traded, which happens on no day of this trip, and that last order is 15:45 while the kitchen only serves lunch between 11:00 and 14:00, which the food card says where it is read.

notes: A proper western-style kitchen inside the Tenri City Trail Center, which is to say on the Yamanobe-no-michi itself, at the midpoint just past Chogaku-ji. The lunch set meals are hamburg steak at 1,800 yen, fried prawns at 1,800 for three and 2,400 for five, and grilled black-wagyu loin at 2,400. Breakfast runs 09:00 to 10:00 and lunch and cafe 11:00 to 16:30, Tuesday to Sunday; the lunch menu changes at 14:00 and set meals stop at 15:30. Dinner, 17:00 to 21:00 with last order 20:30, runs only Thursday to Sunday and on public holidays. Monday is different rather than closed: an 11:00 to 14:00 "kimagure" lunch only, and when a Monday falls on a public holiday that lunch moves to the Tuesday. The first Monday of the month is the exception — the Trail Center itself is shut and so is the restaurant. About a kilometre from Yanagimoto station on the Manyo-Mahoroba line.

notes: A station canteen inside Yanagimoto station on the Manyo-Mahoroba line — plain and fast, 10:00 to 15:00. It is shut on Mondays and Tuesdays, and when either of those falls on a public holiday it trades and takes the Wednesday off instead — which happens once inside these dates: Tuesday 3 November is Culture Day, so the shop is open that day and closed on Wednesday 4 November. Yanagimoto is the walk's first bail-out station, about twenty minutes on from the Trail Center, so this doubles as the landing point if the day is cut short. The pin is the station building itself.

notes: A curry house of 26 seats in the Mochiidono covered arcade, a few minutes south of Kintetsu Nara station: spinach and tomato and spice, plus coconut chicken, Yamato beef, baked and omelette curries, a curry ramen, and vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and pork-free versions. It trades straight through, 11:30 to 20:00, with no midday break — Wednesday is the one short day, 11:30 to 15:30. The cutoffs are earlier than the doors and follow whichever close applies: last in 19:25 and last order 19:30 on a 20:00 day, last in 14:55 and last order 15:00 on the Wednesday. There is no closing day at all — the shop added Thursday trading on 1 June 2026 and says so on its own page. Everything is cooked to order, so nothing sells out. Payment is unusually broad: six card brands, PayPay, LINE Pay, au Pay, d-barai, WeChat Pay, Alipay, QUICPay, iD and ICOCA. The evening end is given as 20:30 on one listing and 20:00 on the shop's own page; the narrower is recorded here.

notes: Direct-flame kamameshi — rice cooked to order in its own iron pot over a flame — from a house that has been doing it in Nara for sixty years. This is the park branch, in Nara Park itself near the national museum, and it is the one Nara-city lunch that needs no walk west into the arcades. 43 seats. The times recorded here are the ones the shop publishes, and they are last orders rather than closing times: 11:00 to 15:00 on weekdays and 11:00 to 16:00 at weekends and on public holidays. Allow time for the pot after ordering — it is cooked from raw. Takeaway kamameshi from 1,300 yen. The shop prints its street address without a postal code, so none is shipped; there is no mapped node for it either, and the pin is the land-registry point for the address, which falls in the same postal block as the museum, about 250 metres away.

notes: A soba house at reasonable money on the Kibune lane by the Hongu shrine, 11:00 to 17:00, closed Thursdays — a single fixed closing day on a lane where most of the neighbours are course-menu ryokan kitchens taking bookings. That is what makes it usable: it is a walk-in noodle house exactly where the day needs one, on the way down the valley from the ridge crossing. Soba is the whole menu. The shop stopped serving the kamameshi it used to be known for in 2022 and says its soba line-up changes with the season — its own channel now calls it Soba Denbe, while the gnavi listing cited above still advertises the old dish. It shuts when the soba runs out rather than at a fixed hour, and opens somewhere between 11:00 and 11:30 depending on the day, so the 17:00 here is a ceiling and not a promise. Reservations are refused outright and seating is in arrival order; cards, electronic money and QR are all refused. Fifty-two seats, twelve downstairs and forty up. It has the river-platform seating the lane is known for, with the water running close under the tables — but that is a summer arrangement, so in November the meal is indoors. Twenty-four minutes on foot from Kibuneguchi station. There is no mapped node for the shop; the pin is the land-registry point for the address, which reverse-geocodes to the right block of Kurama-Kibune-cho.

Cake sets from 1,280 yen and a matcha parfait at 1,980 — but from October to May it also runs a food menu, which is the half of the year this trip falls in, so it is a lunch and not only a sweet stop. That menu is four dishes and it is not cheap: wild-boar kamameshi at 2,200 yen, which is cooked from raw and takes about twenty minutes, a wild-boar and egg-yolk rice bowl at 1,700, Kyoto yuba over rice at 1,550, and a limited daily run of wild-boar curry at 1,300. Only one listing carries that food menu at all — the tourism-board page and the older city guides show the sweets and nothing else — so the four figures rest on a single source and should be read as approximate. Closing days are irregular and the shop announces them only on its own Instagram. From Kibuneguchi station it is four minutes on the Kyoto bus to the Kibune stop and ten minutes on foot; there is no car park. Its street number is given as 74 on the tourism-board page and as 76 on the aggregators; 74 is what the mapped node carrying the shop name shows, and that node is the pin here.

address_jp: 〒616-8292 京都府京都市右京区梅ケ畑高雄町5
notes: A teahouse founded in 1952, standing on the Jingo-ji approach about half way up the stone steps and below the mountain gate, beside the inkstone rock it is named for, so that the climb to the temple and the walk back down both pass its door — roughly ninety-five metres above the Takao bridge and ninety-eight below the gate. 09:00 to 17:00. Closing days are irregular in principle, but the house publishes two rules that remove the doubt for this trip: no closures at all in November, and shut for January and February. The menu is mountain teahouse food — nabeyaki udon 1,400 yen, yuba soba or udon and mountain-vegetable momiji soba 1,000, herring soba 1,250, tempura 1,000, kitsune 750, and in autumn only a set of yudofu, a simmered dish, seasoned rice, momiji tempura and pickles at 1,900. The house sweet, momiji-mochi, is 700 and matcha with a sweet 850, and one published restriction touches the sweet rather than the meal: in autumn the momiji-mochi may be suspended between 11:00 and 14:00. Its listing states that cards, electronic money and QR are all refused. No seat count is published on any channel, so none is given here. The pin is the mapped node bearing the shop name; the land-parcel centroid for Takao-cho 5 covers Jingo-ji as well and was not used.

address_jp: 〒616-8277 京都府京都市右京区梅ヶ畑高雄町 神護寺境内
notes: A light-meal and tea house on the Jingo-ji approach, 09:00 to 17:00. Closing days are irregular in principle, but the Takao preservation association's own member list states that it does not close at all from October to early December — a window that covers this whole trip, which is why this card shows it open. The association lists the house under light meals, tea and room hire, and the three things it prints are all momiji dishes: matcha with momiji-mochi 600 yen, yuzu momiji udon or soba 800, and two-colour soba, mugwort and plum, with seasonal rice 1,200. The udon and the rice cakes are made in-house, and the house claims body in its noodles. Cards and electronic money are both refused and QR payment is accepted; neither the association list nor the Tabelog entry prints a seat count, so none is given here. The association gives the address as inside the Jingo-ji precinct; the pin is the building carrying the shop name on the map, which sits on the steps roughly fifty metres from Suzuriishi-tei and at much the same height, not at the temple end of the approach. No source states which of the two is passed first, and on the mapped nodes they are level, so treat them as one stop. Its hours and its season rule are second-hand: the shop publishes nothing of its own, and both come from that member list, hence the medium confidence.

notes: A house founded in the 1910s, directly in front of Kinpusen-ji's Zao-do, 09:00 to 17:00, closed Wednesdays — a single fixed closing day, which makes it the most dependable meal on the Yoshino ridge, and its Tabelog entry adds that it does not close at all during November. 63 seats, 45 at tables and 18 on tatami, so it absorbs walk-ins on a busy autumn day — though the plainer house a few doors along is larger still, at 66 inside and 6 on a terrace. Kakinoha-zushi, the leaf-wrapped pressed sushi that mountain pilgrims carried on this ridge, plus udon and soba sets and seasonal set meals; the windows look out over the ridge the cherries cover in spring. Its two channels contradict each other on cards — the shop's own listing names JCB and Tabelog names American Express, and neither names Visa or Mastercard — so this is a cash meal in practice. The kakinoha-zushi-making class needs a telephone booking the day before; eating there does not, and no table can be reserved at all. Parking is one more disagreement, two spaces on one channel and none on the other, which changes nothing on foot. The number recorded here is the one printed on the shop's own listing.

The association also prints the seating, 66 places inside and 6 on a terrace — more than the better-known house it stands beside, which has 63. Its closing days are irregular on both channels and neither publishes a policy, which is stated rather than smoothed over; checking it costs nothing because it is next door to the alternative.

notes: A rice-bowl house at the station end of Komachi-dori, the sister shop of Kawagoeya, founded in 1887, and it cooks with the same kaeshi the parent house has handed down. Tempura bowls are what it is built on — the large-prawn tendon and the house tendon — alongside the shirasu bowl that is Kamakura's own dish, an eel bowl and a mixed seafood bowl; the whitebait is landed in Sagami Bay and the rest of the fish comes from the Yokohama market. Forty seats, eight at the counter and thirty-two at tables. Prices from its own menu page: shirasu bowl 1,430 yen, large-prawn tendon 2,100, tempura set 2,580, eel bowl 3,000, house tendon 3,500. Closed Wednesdays. Cards are not accepted. CONFLICT ON THE HOURS, and it is the one figure this record is chosen for: the shop's own page states eleven to eight straight through in words — toshi-eigyo — and the Kamakura City Tourism Association prints the same band with last order at seven, while a commercial directory prints a split service, eleven to three and five to ten, with a two-hour midday break. Two channels that the shop controls or that the city publishes agree against one aggregator, and the aggregator also miscategorises the shop as a soba house and gives a closing hour two hours later than the shop's own, so the continuous band is what ships. The practical effect is handled by arriving a little after five rather than before it, which works under either reading. Three minutes on foot from the east exit of Kamakura station, and the pin is the national geospatial authority's street-number point for Komachi 2-10-1, 153 metres from the station record. No rating channel carries this shop: no Tabelog score was found for it, and it holds no Hyakumeiten or Michelin listing, so unlike most of the food roster its standing rests on the house record and the city tourism association rather than on a score.

Eleven to nine Monday to Thursday and eleven to ten Friday, Saturday and Sunday; the same later close is printed for public holidays, which the seven weekday fields here cannot express, so on a holiday falling Monday to Thursday the card understates the closing hour by an hour. No closing day is printed at all — the shop keeps the ekie building's own calendar, which is not published far enough ahead to read here. The postcode and street number are the ekie building's as its operator prints them; the shop's own page gives only the floor. The pin is the ekie building rather than a shop door, so the offset is vertical rather than horizontal; it is the national geospatial authority point for the building address, which reverse-geocodes into Matsubaracho with the operator's own postcode, and the map node carrying the name ekie sits about seventy metres away in the neighbouring Enkobashicho and was not used.

The shop's own site gives hours but no closing day, so the closing day and the seat count come from the two editorial channels also cited here, which agree.

notes: A shop that calls itself, on its own site, the only place on Miyajima handling oysters alone — its claim, not an independent survey, though the island's most prominent oyster house, Yakigaki no Hayashi, publishes a menu page headed "dishes other than oysters" (tonkatsu, ebi-fry, udon, soba, anago-meshi). In the middle of the Omotesando shopping street about ten minutes from the ferry pier, started by a craftsman who had spent forty years grilling oysters on the island. Its own site says it appears in the Michelin guide for the Hiroshima area. A hundred and ten seats including tatami, with a maximum of sixty seated for a party. Ten to six with last order at six — an hour later than Yakigaki no Hayashi's Sunday close and ninety minutes past its last order — but the shop qualifies that band three ways itself: the hours vary by season, irregular closing days occur, and it may close early once the oysters run out, so the card prints when it trades and refuses to assert that it is open. Its two channels give different postcodes, 739-0588 on the shop's own site and 739-0558 on its directory listing; the shop's own is what ships. The telephone number is the relay number that listing prints. The name is written 牡蠣屋.

The postcode and street number are the ekie building's as its operator prints them; the shop's page gives only the floor and the hall. The pin is the ekie building, so the offset from the counter is vertical; it is the national geospatial authority point for the building address, which reverse-geocodes into Matsubaracho with the operator's own postcode, and the map node carrying the name ekie sits about seventy metres away in the neighbouring Enkobashicho and was not used.

notes: A chanko house inside Ryogoku Edo NOREN, eighty-eight seats, with the whole room available for a private booking. Lunch eleven to three with last order at two, dinner five to ten with last order at nine.
